subject: 개인 동일성과 시간
title: What makes a person the same over time
content: A person at seventy shares almost no material with the child she once was, and her beliefs, tastes, and memories have changed as thoroughly as her cells. Yet we hold her responsible for what that child promised and we call the two one person. Moral philosophy asks what this identity consists in, and the question is not idle, since responsibility, punishment, and obligation all presuppose an answer. One tradition locates identity in memory. A later self is the same person as an earlier one if it remembers being that earlier self, and the chain of such memories carries identity forward. The account fits our ordinary judgments, and it explains why we hesitate to blame someone who has genuinely forgotten. Its difficulty is that memory is unreliable and comes in degrees, so identity would come in degrees too, which is not how we treat it in law or in morality. A second tradition points to bodily continuity, arguing that identity requires an unbroken physical history however much the parts are replaced. This avoids the problems of memory, yet it delivers verdicts many find unacceptable in cases where the body persists while the person seems obviously gone. Some philosophers conclude that no single criterion will serve, and that the truth about identity is less determinate than our moral practices assume. If they are right, then what needs revising is not the metaphysics but the confidence with which we hold people to their past.

subject: 타인의 마음을 어떻게 아는가
title: Knowledge of other minds
content: Each of us knows directly that we have experiences, yet nobody has direct access to anyone else's. What we observe in others is behaviour and physiology, and from these we infer an inner life we can never inspect. Philosophers have long asked what justifies that inference, and the question is more serious than it first appears, since almost every moral judgment we make assumes that others can suffer. The traditional answer argues from analogy. I notice that my own pain produces certain expressions, I observe those expressions in another, and I conclude that a similar experience lies behind them. Critics reply that this is an inductive argument from a single case, which is the weakest form the inference can take, and that no amount of care will strengthen it. A different response denies that any inference is needed. On this view we perceive emotion in a face rather than deducing it, and the demand for a justifying argument imports a picture of the mind as hidden behind behaviour, a picture that is itself the source of the trouble. What gives the question moral weight is that our answers vary with the case. We extend confident attributions to those who resemble us and hesitate as the resemblance decreases, and that hesitation has consequences for how we treat animals, infants, and people whose expressions we misread. The epistemology and the ethics are not separable here.

subject: 기술이 만드는 새로운 책임
title: Moral responsibility and new technology
content: Our moral vocabulary developed for actions whose consequences were near in space and time and whose authors were identifiable. A person struck another, and both the harm and its cause were plain to everyone. Technology has since produced situations that fit this pattern badly, and the resulting gaps in responsibility are not merely legal puzzles but genuine difficulties for ethics. Consider a harm that emerges from a system nobody designed as a whole. Each engineer made a defensible choice, each user acted reasonably, and yet the injury arose from their interaction. Our ordinary moral concepts want to locate a culprit, and when they cannot they suggest that no wrong occurred, which is plainly the wrong conclusion. Some philosophers therefore extend responsibility to those who could have foreseen the risk even if they did not cause the harm directly. Others argue that we need a notion of collective responsibility which does not reduce to individual blame. A second difficulty concerns scale. An action whose effect is negligible taken alone becomes serious when multiplied by millions, and the moral status of that individual act is unclear. Saying that each contributor does no wrong yields the absurd result that a grave harm was produced by nothing but permissible acts. These candidate solutions all revise something we would rather keep, which is a sign that the problem is real rather than a confusion to be cleared away.

subject: 흑사병 이후의 임금과 토지
title: Wages and land after the medieval plague
content: The plague that swept medieval Europe in the middle of the fourteenth century killed a large share of the people within a few years, and its results are visible in the records that survive. Land that had been scarce became plentiful next to the workers left to farm it, while labour that had been cheap became dear. Manor accounts from the decades after this show wages rising and rents falling, and they show lords struggling to hold the tenants who could now find better terms elsewhere. What followed was not a simple gain for those who lived through it. Rulers across the region therefore answered with laws that fixed wages at their older levels and forbade workers to leave their manors, and the courts of the period are full of cases brought under them. This attempt to legislate against the new scarcity shows how sharply the balance had shifted, and it bred the resentments that surface in the revolts of the next generation. The longer results differed by region, and that difference is telling. Where lords held power together, dues were tightened and serfdom hardened; where towns were strong and tenants could move, dues eroded and rents fell into money. The same shock therefore produced opposite outcomes a few hundred miles apart, which suggests that it set the terms while older arrangements decided what happened within them.

subject: 보편적 인권 주장의 난점
title: Difficulties in the claim to universal rights
content: The claim that certain rights belong to every person regardless of where they live is among the most consequential moral assertions of the modern era, and it faces objections that its defenders have not fully answered. The first is historical. The vocabulary of rights emerged from particular traditions, and critics argue that presenting it as universal disguises a local morality as a discovery about humanity. Defenders reply that the origin of an idea does not settle its validity, since mathematics also arose somewhere. A second objection is more difficult. Rights are claims against someone, and a claim without an addressee is empty. Where a right to food or education is asserted, it is unclear who bears the corresponding duty, and an obligation that falls on everyone in general may fall on no one in particular. Some philosophers restrict genuine rights to those that require others merely to refrain from acting, since duties of non-interference have a clear bearer. Others accept the wider list and argue that institutions rather than individuals bear the duty. What keeps the debate alive is that both the objections and the claim answer to something real. Moral judgment does seem to reach across borders, and yet the machinery that would make such judgments effective is built locally. Universal rights therefore name an aspiration whose justification is contested and whose implementation remains unfinished.

subject: 고대 전쟁과 야금 기술의 관계
title: Ancient warfare and the working of metal
content: Histories of ancient warfare often turn on the appearance of a superior weapon, with bronze giving way to iron and the armies that adopted the new metal prevailing over those that did not. The archaeological record supports a more complicated account. Early iron was not obviously better than good bronze, since it required careful working to exceed the older alloy, and the first iron weapons recovered from ancient sites are frequently inferior to the bronze ones buried alongside them. What iron offered was availability. Bronze required tin, which occurred in few places and travelled long distances along routes that a rival could cut, whereas iron ore was widely distributed and could be worked with local fuel. A community that adopted iron freed itself from a supply line, and that independence mattered more than any advantage in the blade itself. The transition therefore spread fastest where the tin routes were least secure. The consequences reached beyond armies. When weapons no longer depended on a scarce imported metal, the cost of arming a large force fell, and the ancient societies that followed fielded infantry of a size the earlier palace economies had not attempted. Historians accordingly read the shift as a change in who could afford to fight rather than as a change in how effectively they did so, and the political rearrangements of the period follow from that.

subject: 집단 책임은 성립하는가
title: Whether groups can bear moral responsibility
content: We routinely say that a company acted wrongly or that a nation owes an apology, and such statements seem to attribute moral responsibility to a group rather than to any individual within it. Philosophers disagree about whether this is a genuine attribution or a convenient shorthand, and the disagreement has practical weight, since it bears on compensation, punishment, and public apology. The reductive view holds that only individuals can act, so that talk of collective guilt must resolve into claims about particular people. Its appeal is that responsibility has always required agency, and a corporation has no beliefs or intentions of its own. The difficulty is that some group actions cannot be traced to any individual decision. A committee can reach an outcome that no member favoured, and a firm can cause harm through procedures that each employee followed correctly. The non-reductive view accepts collective agents, arguing that a group with a decision procedure can hold commitments and be held to them. Critics answer that this risks letting individuals hide behind the entity, and the worry is not merely theoretical. Where a fine falls on shareholders and no person is answerable, the moral point of blame is lost. Both sides therefore agree about the danger while disagreeing about its source, and the debate turns on whether a group can be blamed without anyone being blamed.

subject: 평등은 무엇의 평등인가
title: Equality of what
content: Almost everyone endorses equality in some form, and this agreement conceals a disagreement about what should be equalized. Income, wealth, opportunity, welfare, and capability have all been proposed, and the choice is not a technical matter, since each answer yields a different judgment about the same distribution. A society that equalizes income will not have equalized welfare if some people need far more resources to reach the same condition. The point is made vivid by disability. Two people with identical incomes are not equally placed if one must spend much of that income on medical care, so equality of resources fails to deliver what its defenders wanted. Equalizing welfare instead runs into a different objection, because it requires transferring more to those with expensive tastes, and most of us think that a person who has cultivated a preference for rare wine has no claim on the rest of us. A middle answer focuses on capability, asking what people are actually able to do and be rather than what they hold or feel. This accommodates disability without rewarding cultivated preference, and it has proved influential in how development is measured. Its critics observe that the list of relevant capabilities must be specified, and that specifying it requires the very judgments about the good life that a theory of justice was meant to avoid making.

subject: 고대 중국의 운하와 조운
title: Canals and grain transport in ancient China
content: Moving grain overland is expensive, because the animals that pull the carts eat a share of what they carry and that share grows with distance. Beyond a few hundred miles the cargo is consumed before it arrives. Water transport removes this limit, and the ancient states that could move grain by canal were able to feed capitals far larger than their immediate hinterlands could support. The canal systems built across ancient China were responses to precisely this constraint. What such works demanded was continuous administration rather than a single act of construction. Canals silt, embankments fail, and locks require attendants, so a waterway that is not maintained becomes useless within a few seasons. The bureaus that survive in the historical record were therefore permanent, with officials assigned to sections, schedules for dredging, and granaries placed along the route where cargoes could be held when the water was low. The engineering was the easier half of the problem. Historians read the condition of these systems as an index of central authority. When the records show canals silting and grain arriving late, the administration was weakening, and political disruption usually follows in the same decades. The relationship runs in both directions, since a capital that could not be fed lost the capacity to govern the provinces that fed it, and the ancient sources describe that spiral more than once.

subject: 위험 감수와 도덕적 운
title: Risk and moral luck
content: Two drivers are equally careless, and one of them happens to strike a pedestrian who steps into the road while the other arrives home without incident. We blame the first far more severely, and the law punishes him far more severely, yet the difference between them lies entirely in something neither controlled. Moral philosophy calls this moral luck, and it is difficult to accept and difficult to reject. Our considered principle says that people should be judged only for what is within their control, and that principle has strong support. Applying it consistently, however, requires us to say that the driver who killed someone is no more blameworthy than the one who did not, and almost nobody can hold that judgment steadily. The intuition that outcomes matter is as firm as the principle that denies it. Several responses have been attempted. Some philosophers accept the principle and treat our differential reactions as an error to be corrected, comparing them to other biases we have learned to discount. Others hold that the outcome reveals the true character of the risk taken, so that the unlucky driver was in fact doing something worse. A third position accepts that moral judgment is simply not governed by control alone, and that the demand for such governance imports an ideal of fairness that morality was never built to satisfy.

subject: 유럽 봉건제의 성립 조건
title: What made medieval lordship possible
content: Medieval lordship in Europe is often described as a system, with obligations flowing upward and protection flowing down in an orderly hierarchy. The documents of the period support no such tidiness. What historians find instead is a patchwork of bargains struck locally between people whose relative strength varied, and the arrangements differ so much from region to region that a single model describes none of them well. Two conditions appear wherever such lordship took hold. The first is the absence of an authority able to guarantee security across a wide area, which left communities dependent on whoever could raise armed men nearby. The second is an economy in which land rather than coin was the usable form of wealth, so that service could be rewarded only by granting the use of an estate. Where either condition failed, the arrangements look different, and the regions with strong towns and circulating money developed obligations paid in cash instead. This explains the variation better than any account that treats lordship as a stage every society passes through. It arose where the conditions held and dissolved when they ceased to, and the medieval centuries during which it dominated were the centuries in which those conditions were widespread. Historians accordingly describe it as a solution to a particular problem rather than as a phase in a sequence.

subject: 전문가 신뢰의 조건
title: When it is rational to trust an expert
content: A person without training cannot evaluate a technical claim on its merits, and yet decisions about health, law, and public policy require such claims to be believed or rejected. This creates a problem in the theory of knowledge that is also a moral problem, since the consequences of misplaced trust fall on those least able to assess it. Simply deferring to whoever holds credentials will not do, because experts disagree and some of them are wrong. What the novice can assess, philosophers have argued, is not the claim but the conditions under which it was produced. Was the field organized so that errors get caught, does the expert have interests that the conclusion happens to serve, and do independent practitioners converge on the same answer? These are questions about the social structure of inquiry rather than about its content, and a person outside the field can investigate them. Trust grounded this way is defeasible and appropriately so. It weakens when the checks are absent, when funding aligns with outcomes, or when apparent agreement turns out to rest on a single source that everyone is citing. The moral obligation that falls on experts follows from the same analysis, since a community that must judge by these signals is entitled to have them be honest ones, and disguising an interest is a wrong distinct from being mistaken.
